title: 防衛費 米要求の3.5%明示見送りへ
body: 安全保障関連3文書の年内の改定で、政府が今後5年間の防衛費の国内総生産（GDP）比について、トランプ米政権が同盟国に求める「3.5%」の目標の明示を見送る方向で検討していることがわかった。関連経費も含めた防衛費の大幅な増額には踏み出す方針で、防衛力強化の姿勢を示すことで米側の理解を得たい考えだ。【写真】高市政権の防衛政策、知らなかった支持者複数の日本政府関係者によると、米国は日本側に対し、GDP比3.5%の防衛費支出が「グローバルスタンダード（世界基準）」だとして、水面下で繰り返し求めてきた。日本が3.5%の明示を見送る背景には財政事情がある。仮に防衛費を3.5%にすれば年20兆円超になり、財源確保のための増税は避けられない。政府・与党内では、負担軽減を図るとして食料品の消費減税を進めておきながら、国民に大きな負担増を強いるのは政治的に難しいとの見方が強い。日本政府内では、米国が、防衛産業基盤などを含む長期的な防衛力の強化を重視しており、「3.5%」の明記に固執しないのではないかとの見方もある。防衛力強化に取り組む姿勢を示すことで、米側の理解を得る考えとみられる。一方、高市早苗首相が安全保障環境の厳しさを理由に防衛力の抜本的強化を打ち出すなか、防衛費については「年10兆円では足りない」（官邸関係者）といった意見が出ており、大幅な増額が見込まれている。

title: 小学校銃撃で子ら4人死亡 米報道
body: アメリカ西部・オレゴン州の小学校で15日、銃乱射事件があり、容疑者が射殺されました。アメリカメディアは、子供3人と大人1人が死亡したと伝えています。【画像】米ニューヨーク中心部で立て続けに銃撃事件　もし巻き込まれたら地元警察によりますと、オレゴン州ベンドにある小学校で15日午後1時頃、「校舎の外で車に向けて発砲している人物がいる」「銃乱射事件が起きている」など複数の通報がありました。警察官が駆けつけた後、銃撃事件の容疑者1人が校舎の中で射殺されました。ただ、誰が容疑者を撃ったのかは確認中だということです。地元警察は、この事件で、子供を含む少なくとも2人がケガをして病院に搬送されていて、容体はわかっていない、としています。一方、CNNとCBSは、子供3人と大人1人が死亡したと伝えています。この小学校には、児童およそ450人と教職員およそ40人が在籍しているということです。捜査当局は銃乱射事件の詳しい状況を調べています。

title: 金融所得を医療費に反映 29年8月
body:
厚生労働省は、７５歳以上の後期高齢者の金融所得を医療費の窓口負担や保険料の算定に反映させる新たな仕組みについて、２０２９年８月に開始する方針を固めた。株式の配当や譲渡益などを把握し、支払い能力に応じた負担に改める。３０年８月から完全実施する。【表】一目でわかる…８月に見直された所得区分ごとの医療費の自己負担額
１６日に開かれる社会保障審議会（厚労相の諮問機関）の医療保険部会で提示する。５月に成立した改正健康保険法で仕組みが盛り込まれ、公布から５年以内に施行するとしていた。
７５歳以上の窓口負担は原則１割で、所得が多いと２割や３割になる。ただ、現在、配当などの金融所得は、確定申告をしなければ市町村の課税所得情報に含まれないため、算定の対象にならず、不公平だとの指摘が出ていた。
同省案では、２９年１月から金融機関に、配当支払いなどの法定調書を都道府県ごとの広域連合にオンラインで提出することを義務化する。法定調書には、株の売買に伴う納税手続きなどを金融機関が代理して行う特定口座の年間取引報告書などもあり、種類ごとに提出期限が定められている。
２９年１月末が提出期限となっている２８年分の法定調書の内容は、２９年８月から窓口負担や保険料に反映される。２９年２月～３０年１月末に提出される２９年分は、３０年８月から反映する。
同省は法定調書データベース（仮称）を構築して税務署や自治体などの情報と連携し、保険料などを算出しやすくする。来年度予算の概算要求に５６億円を計上し、自治体や金融機関のシステム改修費も補助する。

title: 男性市議からセクハラ 申し立て
body: 茨城県水戸市議会の男性市議からキスを迫られるなどしたとして、同市議会の女性市議が「市議会ハラスメントの根絶に関する条例」に基づき袴塚孝雄議長に被害を申し立てていたことが15日、複数の関係者への取材で分かった。申し立てによると、女性市議は8月5日夜、市内の飲食店で、男性市議から「バレーボール協会の顧問に推薦する」と持ちかけられ快諾したところ、「チューしたい」などと迫られた。女性市議は拒絶したものの、翌6日にも関係を迫るショートメッセージサービス(SMS)の連絡が届いた。再び断ったところ、男性市議は市議会常任委員会での女性市議の振る舞いを問題視するようになったという。女性市議は茨城新聞の取材に対し、「悪くて大きなものに巻かれたくない。悪いことは悪いと言いたい」と語った。男性市議は「2人だけで食事したことは一度もない。夢にも思っていない話でびっくり」と女性市議の申し立てに反論している。市議会は、弁護士による申し立て内容を精査した上で、各会派の代表が集まる会議で調査を進める。

title: 風俗店勤務要求疑い 元ホスト逮捕
body: 東京・歌舞伎町の元ホストの男が客からホストクラブの代金を取り立てるために女性客に性風俗店で働くことを強要したとして、警視庁に逮捕されたことがわかりました。【写真を見る】逮捕された元ホスト・竹岡拓人容疑者(27)捜査関係者によりますと、風営法違反の疑いで逮捕されたのは、新宿区歌舞伎町の「AXEL by ACQUA」で、「エレン」という名前でホストをしていた竹岡拓人容疑者（27）です。竹岡容疑者は去年11月、新宿・歌舞伎町の飲食店でホストクラブの20代の女性客に対し、「ヘルスの仕事がある」「売り上げが上がれば早くホストを辞めて2人で旅行に行ったりするお金に使えるから、今だけ頑張ってほしい」と言い、ホストクラブの料金を払わせるため、性風俗店で働いて金を稼ぐよう要求した疑いがもたれています。竹岡容疑者はこの女性とマッチングアプリを通じて知り合いましたが、当初、「IT関係者」と肩書を偽って交際をもちかけ、交際が始まったタイミングで「実は副業でホストをやっている」「俺の全部を知ってほしいから来てほしい」と明かし、ホストクラブに何度も連れて行っていたということです。そして、女性が支払いに困窮すると、竹岡容疑者は職安法違反の疑いで共に逮捕されたスカウトの福重昂宏容疑者（35）を女性に紹介し、女性は千葉県船橋市の性風俗店で働くことになったということです。竹岡容疑者は女性に消費者金融で金を借りさせるなどもしていて、女性は竹岡容疑者の店であわせて380万円ほどを支払ったとみられています。また、別の20代女性も同様の被害にあったと訴えています。女性はJNNの取材に応じ、「風俗は嫌と言ったのに、本人の売り上げに達しないとデートができないと言われ、行っていた」と明かしました。この女性の場合、稼いだ金から生活費を除くほぼ全額を竹岡容疑者のために支払うことになり、その額は半年で1000万円近くに及んだといいます。警視庁は、竹岡容疑者が同様の手口で複数の女性に性風俗店で働くよう要求していたとみて調べています。去年6月に施行された改正風営法では、客を誘惑して料金支払いのため性風俗店で働くよう要求することは禁止行為として明記されていて、警視庁がこの禁止行為で摘発を行うのは初めてだということです。

title: 北朝鮮 14日に潜水艦巡航ミサイル
body: Jack Kim　Joyce Lee[ソウル １５日 ロイター] - 北朝鮮国営の朝鮮中央通信（ＫＣＮＡ）は１５日、海軍の任務遂行能力と戦争抑止力の信頼性を検証するため、潜水艦発射型戦略‌巡航ミサイル２種類の試験を１４日に実施したと報じた。試験は北朝鮮東岸⁠沖で行われ、軍高官らが視察した。試験が近隣諸国の安全保障に悪影響を及ぼさなかったと述べた以外、ミサイルや発射に関する詳細は明​らかにしなかった。北朝鮮は、近代的なミサイル潜水艦と弾道 ・巡航ミサイル開発を推進しており、老朽化した潜水艦を含むさ‌まざまなプラットフォームから試験発射を行っている。今回の試射は、金正恩朝鮮労働党総書記の最優先軍事課題の一つである、信頼性の高い海上核抑‌止力の確立に向けた北朝鮮の最‌新の取り組みだが、アナリストらは、現時点では完全​な作戦能力は実証されていないと指摘している。一方、韓国軍合同参謀本部は１５日、発射を監視‌・追跡したと発表。報道官は、１種類の巡航ミサイルが垂直発射システムから、もう１種類が魚雷発射管から発‌射されたと評価していると明ら​かにした。韓国側のアナリストらは、ＫＣＮＡが公開した潜水艦とミサイル‌発射の様子を捉えた写真から、発射は北朝鮮が２０２３年９月に公開した改良型ディーゼル潜水艦「金君玉⁠英雄」から行われたものとみられると指摘した。韓国防衛安保フォーラムのシン・ジョンウ事務局長は試射について、「実戦配備に向けた戦闘システムの試験が進められている」ことを示⁠していると分析。「近いうちに潜水艦発射弾道ミサイ​ル（ＳＬＢＭ）を発射する可能‌性が高い」と述べた。防衛アナリストらはまた、北朝鮮が１４日に使用した可能性のあるような垂直発射システムにより、潜水艦は魚雷発射管よりも迅速に、かつより大規模⁠な一斉発射が可能となり、防衛側の対応が困難になる可能性があると指⁠摘している。韓国統一研究院のホン・ミン上級研究員は、北朝鮮が今回のイベントを開発試験⁠ではなく「定例の動員準備検査」と表現したのは、潜水艦が配備に向けて進んでいることを示す意‌図があっ⁠たようだと述べた。しかし、水中からの発射、長期間の哨戒、ＳＬＢＭの運用がまだ​実証されていないことから、現時点では「限られた作戦能力」しか持っていないと考えていると付け加えた。

title: 邦人記者拘束 露の狙いを識者指摘
body:
ロシア当局によって日本人記者が拘束されました。ロシアの国営メディアが報じたのは、黒い制服姿の職員がホテルの部屋に踏み込み、中にいた日本人記者をスパイ容疑で拘束した際の様子だとする映像です。日本人記者は今後どうなるのか、そして、日本はどう対応していくべきなのか、日本テレビ・小林史解説委員の解説です。【動画】専門家「ここまでやるのは非常にレアなケース」、ロシア拘束 “スパイ容疑” 日本人記者の今後は？　12月まで勾留決定
今回の拘束はとにかく異例で、専門家も「日本人に対してここまでやるのは非常にレアなケース」と驚いています。ロシア政治に詳しい廣瀬陽子教授は、記者は“捕虜交換の人質”として拘束された可能性もあり、今回、動画を世界中に公開したのは、見せしめとしてロシアに不利益な報道に対するけん制もあるのではと指摘しています。今回、拘束されたのは、ロシアのユジノサハリンスクに駐在していた北海道新聞の男性記者で、ロシア当局は、北方領土などにおける情報収集が「ジャーナリストの範囲を大きく逸脱していた」と説明。さらに、「日本の情報機関からの指示で動いていた」とも主張していて、12月まで勾留されることが決まりました。
ロシア国営のタス通信は、記者はこのあと非公開の裁判にかけられ、収監が続く可能性があると報じています。過去の事例をみてみますと、2023年にはウォール・ストリート・ジャーナルのアメリカ人記者がスパイ容疑で拘束されています。この記者も、はじめは2か月の勾留が言い渡されましたが、結局、釈放されたのは1年5か月後でした。しかもこの釈放は、ロシア人スパイとの身柄交換を条件に実現した形です。日本人記者の今後も、日本がどこまでロシア側と交渉できるかが焦点になりそうです。外務省は14日夕方、駐日ロシア大使を呼び出し、速やかな情報提供と公平な扱いをロシア側に求めた上で、ロシア側の一方的な発信などに強く抗議しました。

title: 米大統領 機密情報漏れ説明し不満
body:
【ワシントン共同】トランプ米大統領は14日、対イラン軍事作戦で機密情報が漏れた実例があるとして不満を示し、メディアにリークした人物は「銃殺されるべきだ」と述べた。米憲法で定められた報道の自由に後ろ向きな姿勢を改めて鮮明にした。西部アリゾナ州での支持者集会で語った。【写真】ビル・ゲイツ氏が暴露したトランプ氏の「無知さ」　18年記事
トランプ氏は、未公表の軍事作戦の内容がメディアに漏れたために計画の変更を強いられたことがあったと説明。内部情報を漏らした者に対し「昔は銃殺していた」とし、極めて厳しい処分を科すべきだと訴えた。政権に否定的な報道をしたメディアについて「情報源を捏造している」と一方的に主張。「情報をリークした人間とほぼ同じくらい悪い」と非難した。

title: トランプ氏 銃殺刑の配信計画中止
body:
【ワシントン共同】トランプ米大統領は15日、殺人罪などで死刑判決を受けた米軍の元少佐の男の銃殺刑を生配信する計画について、中止したと交流サイト（SNS）で明らかにした。超党派の議員や国内外の世論の強い反発を受けて判断したとみられる。【写真】ビル・ゲイツ氏が暴露したトランプ氏の「無知さ」　18年記事
トランプ氏は、銃殺刑の様子を「世界に示すことは強力な抑止力になる」と主張。一方で「多くの善良な人々は生配信を望んでいない」とし、銃殺刑は執行するが、生配信はしないとした。被害者遺族らが執行に立ち会うことは認めるとした。生配信計画はヘグセス国防長官主導で進んでいた。男は2009年に米陸軍基地で銃を乱射して13人を殺害したニダル・マリク・ハサン元少佐で、トランプ氏が銃殺刑を承認。事件が起きた南部テキサス州のフォートフッド陸軍基地で12月3日に執行される予定。国防総省のパーネル報道官は生配信中止についてトランプ氏とヘグセス氏が協議したと説明し、「ヘグセス氏は決定を支持しており、両者の意見は完全に一致している」とした。

title: 小学校銃撃で子ら4人死亡 米報道
body: アメリカ西部・オレゴン州の小学校で15日、銃乱射事件があり、容疑者が射殺されました。アメリカメディアは、子供3人と大人1人が死亡したと伝えています。【画像】米ニューヨーク中心部で立て続けに銃撃事件　もし巻き込まれたら地元警察によりますと、オレゴン州ベンドにある小学校で15日午後1時頃、「校舎の外で車に向けて発砲している人物がいる」「銃乱射事件が起きている」など複数の通報がありました。警察官が駆けつけた後、銃撃事件の容疑者1人が校舎の中で射殺されました。ただ、誰が容疑者を撃ったのかは確認中だということです。地元警察は、この事件で、子供を含む少なくとも2人がケガをして病院に搬送されていて、容体はわかっていない、としています。一方、CNNとCBSは、子供3人と大人1人が死亡したと伝えています。この小学校には、児童およそ450人と教職員およそ40人が在籍しているということです。捜査当局は銃乱射事件の詳しい状況を調べています。

title: 洗濯機が発火恐れ パナがリコール
body: パナソニックは15日、製造販売したドラム式洗濯乾燥機約64万台について、発火の恐れがあるとして部品のリコール（無償点検・修理）を実施する、と発表した。製品から発煙・発火する事故が国内で6件、台湾で1件発生している。けが人はいなかったという。【動画】台所ラップで見つけた物理法則　モバイルバッテリー発火の解決にも？対象となるのは、2021年8月から25年7月までに製造された「LXシリーズ」の21製品で、国内では62万2527台、台湾向けでは1万8144台。洗剤や柔軟剤を入れる「自動投入ユニット」の不具合で、タンクから液体が洗濯槽の外に漏れ出すことが原因。パナソニックでは「当面は洗剤の自動投入機能の使用は控え、タンクを空にして手動で投入してほしい」と呼び掛けている。24年4月に埼玉県内で発生した火災では、今回のリコールの対象となっている洗濯乾燥機本体が焼損したほか、建物1棟が全焼し、5棟が類焼した。部品交換や修理などの問い合わせは専用窓口（0120・878・303）へ。午前9時～午後6時で、12月27日までは毎日受け付ける。（武井風花）

title: サイゼリヤ株 一時14%高の急反発
body:
サイゼリヤの株価が10月15日、大幅に反発した。前日終値6550円から一時920円（14.04%）高の7470円まで上昇し、1カ月ぶりの高値水準をつけた。【画像】サイゼリヤ株、値上げ受け株価大幅反発。「ミラノ風ドリア」はいくらになる？同社は10月14日に、10月29日からのメニュー値上げと2027年8月期の大幅増益計画を同時に発表した。前期は原価高で計画未達だったものの、値上げによる収益改善への期待から買いが集まった。
値上げはメニュー全般で平均6%となる。看板商品の「ミラノ風ドリア」は税込300円から320円に、400円のメニューは420〜430円になる。レジャー施設周辺や都市部の24店舗は平均10%上げる。一方、同社が推す「フレッシュワイン」と、「ランチ」「モーニング限定メニュー」の価格は据え置く。同社は、原材料やエネルギーのコスト上昇が続くなか価格維持に努めてきたが、「当社の努力不足により」原価上昇を吸収できなくなったと説明。利用客に理解を求めた。決算短信によると、メニュー価格を維持する従来の方針を改め、今後は状況に応じて価格を見直すとしている。
2027年8月期の連結業績予想は、売上高が前期比11%増の3337億円、営業利益が29%増の212億円、純利益が21%増の134億円とした。値上げで国内既存店売上高は6%増を見込み、国内の粗利益率は52.1%、国内の営業利益は100億円を計画する。出店は国内外で123店の純増を計画し、設備投資は248億円と前期から2割弱増やす。年間配当は前期と同じ35円。
2026年8月期の連結業績は、売上高が17%増の3014億円、営業利益が6%増の164億円、純利益が1%減の110億円だった。売上高は会社計画を上回ったが、利益は4月に修正した計画に届かなかった。客数は14%増の3億4172万人と好調で、直近の26年9月も国内既存店売上高は前年同月比10.6%増と堅調だ。一方、売上原価率は43.7%と1.8ポイント悪化した。国内では円安やハンバーグ、チキンなどの仕入れ単価上昇、物流費の増加が重なり、原価で約44億円の減益要因となった。中国などアジアの営業利益も4%減の97億円にとどまった。※本記事は、事例として取り上げた金融商品の売買を勧めるものではありません。本記事に記載した情報によって読者に発生した損害や損失に関しては、発行媒体は一切責任を負いません。投資における最終決定はご自身の判断で行ってください。※株価データは2026年10月15日時点。

title: 「お得感」前面に ローソン好調
body:
コンビニエンスストア大手３社の２０２６年８月中間連結決算が１５日、出そろった。国内チェーン全店売上高は、セブン―イレブン・ジャパンとローソンが前年同期を上回った一方、ファミリーマートは下回った。物価高を受けた消費者の節約志向の高まりに対し、各社は割安な弁当を投入するなど商品展開を強化するが、業界全体では来店客数の減少などの課題に直面している。【表】一目でわかる…コンビニ大手が打ち出す新型店舗
ローソンの竹増貞信社長は１５日に東京都内で開いた決算発表の記者会見で、コンビニ業界を取り巻く環境について「厳しい」と指摘した上で、「先手先手で施策を打てるかどうかが問われている」と説明した。
ローソンの国内全店売上高は、８月中間決算では前年同期比１・８％増の１兆３５７６億円だった。弁当などの一部商品の内容量を増やして「お得感」を前面に出すキャンペーンが消費者に受け入れられたほか、ＡＩ（人工知能）システムを使った商品発注の精度が上がったことも奏功した。
最大手のセブン―イレブンもレジ横で販売しているファストフードなどの販売が伸び、全店売上高は１・６％増の２兆８１０３億円だった。
一方、ファミマは、全店売上高が０・６％減の１兆６８４７億円となった。ファミマはローソンと同様、「お得感」を打ち出した弁当、サンドイッチなどの商品展開を進めたが、売上高の増加にはつながらなかった。全店売上高が前年同期を下回った理由について、ファミマの浦島宣哉専務執行役員は１４日の決算発表の会見で、「お客様のニーズを捉えきれていない」と振り返った。
３～８月の国内来店客数（既存店ベース）は、ファミマが前年同期を割り込んだほか、セブン―イレブンも５月以外は前年同月を下回った。節約志向の高まりによって客足が遠のいた可能性がある。この状況に対し、６月以外は前年同月を上回ったローソンの竹増社長は、「欲しい商品が欲しい時にある」店舗作りが来店客数の増加につながるとの見方を示した。

title: ネトフリ 従業員約1000人を削減へ
body: Prathik Jayaprakash　Anzar Mehraj[１４日 ロイター] - 米動画配信大手ネットフリックスが、全従業員の６％に相当‌する約１０００人を削減する。ロイターが入⁠手した社内メモで明らかになった。人員削減は２０２２年以来の規模となる。グレッグ・​ピーターズ、テッド・サランドス両共同最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）が１４日に社員に‌送った電子メールによると、人員削減の大部分は製品、技術、法務、人事の各部‌門が対象となる。ネッ‌トフリックス株は年初来で約２５％下落​しているが、１４日は０．７％上昇した。２０２５年末時点の従業員数は約１万６０００人だった。ユーチュ‌ーブや「ＴｉｋＴｏｋ（ティックトック）」といったプラットフォームが、‌無料で視聴可能な​ユーザー生成コンテンツで視聴者を‌引きつけており、ネットフリックスに対してコス⁠ト面で優位に立っている。さらに、ワーナー・ブラザース・ディスカバリーの配信・スタジオ資産⁠買収が失敗に終わったことで、​ネットフリッ‌クスの戦略に対する懸念がさらに深まった。調査会社イーマーケッターのシニアアナリスト、⁠ロス・ベネス氏は「ネットフリックスは⁠別の主要な収益源を見つけられていない」と指摘。「⁠最終的には、サブスクリプションが頭打ちに近づいている‌ため、⁠収益を多様化する別の収益源が必要に​なるだろう。だが、そこで苦戦が続いている」と述べた。

title: 年金だけで暮らせず 毎日働く71歳
body:
定年後も働く高齢者が増えています。大学卒業後に“安定した会社”で働いてきたという71歳の男性は今、地方のアパートで一人暮らし。「支給される年金だけでは暮らしていけない」と毎日仕事に向かいます。一方、「ずっとこの仕事を続けたい」と話すのはかつて専業主婦だった75歳の女性です。年金で悠々自適に暮らしたいと多くの人が願う“老後”ですが、今や65歳以上の4人に1人が働く時代。働く目的は人それぞれですが、その背景にはなにがあるのでしょうか？「転勤に翻弄されました」見知らぬ土地で追い詰められた妻、子育て世帯と転勤リスク　#マイノーマル
福島県いわき市の8畳ほどのアパートで一人暮らしをする阿部義秀さん（仮名・71歳）はいつも午後6時に就寝します。翌朝午前1時に起床し、仕事へ向かいます。「新聞配達やっています。寝坊したら大変だから」この日の夕食は自分で炊いた米飯と近くのスーパーで買ってきた402円のきんぴらごぼうと167円の2個入りコロッケの残り。いつも、昼食と夕食で同じ総菜を半分ずつ分けて食べると言います。「買い物行っても前と全然違いますよ。前はもっと安い値段で買えた。総菜をカゴに入れても、戻してしまうことが増えたかな…。」阿部さんに支給される年金は月10万円ほど。食費は年々上がり続け、電気やガスなどの光熱費も値上がりしています。寒くなるこれからの時期は暖房費も家計を圧迫します。「新聞配達で稼いだお金がなければ生活できない…。」
阿部さんは都内の大学を卒業後、旧国鉄（日本国有鉄道）の関連会社に就職しました。長男だった阿部さんは就職の際、「安定した企業」という点を最優先にしたと言います。「国鉄関連の会社だったから潰れないだろうと思ってね。国鉄のOBさんが会社の社長になっていたしね。」阿部さんはその会社で25年働きますが、故郷のいわき市に住む父が他界したことをきっかけに帰郷します。「長男としてやるべきこと」との思いから、一人で暮らす母親の面倒をみるためでした。地元の派遣会社に勤めながら、9年間一緒に暮らしました。2011年に母が他界し、阿部さんは次第に老後について考え始めるようになったといいます。「若い頃は老後のことなんて考えてなかったな。年金で暮らしていけるのかなと思っていたんだけど、ちょっと厳しいかもと思うようになって…。」定年後に支給される年金は家賃と光熱費などでほとんどなくなってしまいました。ギャンブルなどに夢中になった時期もあり、僅かですが借金が残っていました。高齢者の住居確保の支援をしているNPOに身元保証になってもらい家賃数万円のアパートに引っ越すなど、生活費を切り詰める日々を送っています。

title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
summary: Trump said some would "rather not watch" the killing of Nidal Hasan, the first military execution in over 60 years.
body:
Thirteen US soldiers were killed in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood in Texas
US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.
Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, whileVice-President JD Vance cast doubton whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.
Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added in the post on Truth Social.
Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US military personnel and injured 32 others at a military base in Texas in 2009. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish.
"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.
After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others.  The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent".
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".
'We'll make sure people can watch Hasan execution' - Hegseth
But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.
The president also called Hasan "totally nuts".
"I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said.
After Trump announced he called it off, a Pentagon spokesman said Hegseth had spoken with the US president beforehand.
"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," the spokesman Sean Parnell said.
John Galligan, a lawyer for Hasan working primarily on civil issues, told the BBC that Trump's decision to cancel the livestream of his execution "comes as no surprise".
"It was initially a dumb decision and statement by Hegseth to livestream any execution - and it violated the Army's own regulation," Galligan said.
He said Hasan is paralysed from the chest down, something that Trump "allegedly didn't even know" when he approved the livestream plan.
"The damage has already been done - the Army is now just trying to clean up the mess," Galligan said. "It will permanently remain a stain on our military justice system."
He added that it was not clear if Hasan was aware yet of Trump's "reversal" of the livestream decision.
Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
US military law requires that a military execution be approved by the US president.
It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward.

title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
summary: Ukraine's president says a pause on striking energy sites is over following fresh Russian attacks.
body:
Ukraine's President Zelensky accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing about Russian strikes to place pressure on Kyiv
Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.
Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We're done,"he told the Financial Times,external.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied - but there had been no "significant damage".
Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks but Ukrainian defence sources later told the BBC some functionality on Starlink satellite services had resumed.
They said "operation while on the move", part of Starlink's military service Starshield, had been restored, although it remains unclear whether restrictions on the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted.
Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added.
In a separate development, seven people are missing aftera drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania, according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them.
Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.
According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.
Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.
He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.
But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.
Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.
European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake".
"Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."
He added: "Peace will be achieved when Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."
Zelensky met Nato chief Mark Rutte as a two-day summit of European leaders began in Brussels on Thursday. The head of the military alliance said they had discussed "the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire as well as Nato allies' continuous support for Ukraine".
Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".
Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.
There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggestedit was the Trump administration's doing.
"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.
Zelensky has questioned Trump's relationship with Russia President, Vladimir Putin
Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street -who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv.
The Ukrainian president told the newspaper he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.
Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.
Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Putin.
He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week: "We didn't destroy any relationship."
Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.
Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.
But he criticised theagreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.
Two people were killed in Sloviansk, Donetsk, after overnight strikes, where a number of residential buildings were destroyed
That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.
Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."
With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.
Local officials report at least 13 people were killed across Ukraine on Wednesday in what Zelensky called a "constant", large-scale Russian attack. He said more than 850 drones had been launched at dozens of cities and communities.
At least three people were killed in the central region of Kirovohrad as it suffered its largest attack since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, officials there said, with nearly 360 drones launched during a 10-hour barrage. Deaths were also reported in Donetsk, Kherson and Volyn.
"It is clear that Russia deliberately escalated these attacks, taking advantage of the easing of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media.

title: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
summary: Two people were airlifted to hospital but no-one's life appeared to be in danger, officials said.
body:
Watch: BBC at scene as emergency crews head towards Channel Tunnel crash
A bus has hit a stationary freight train near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, French authorities say.
The bus, which was carrying lorry drivers due to take a shuttle rail service, struck the train at the loading platform of the tunnel in Coquelles, near Calais, at 19:27 (18:27 BST) on Thursday.
The bus driver and one passenger were severely injured and evacuated by helicopter. None of the injuries were life threatening, a local official said.
Local sub-prefect Agathe Cury said freight and Eurostar passenger traffic through the tunnel had not been disrupted after a brief stoppage to evacuate injured people. An investigation has begun.
Trains near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel (file image)
"Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that had previously been loaded was departing," Cury said.
"For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train.
"The bus did not overturn, it is still upright – but the shock and the collision caused injuries to the people involved."
The incident involved a minibus transporting workers who were about to board Le Shuttle. All were men of different nationalities, she added.
It is not clear whether any British nationals are among the injured.
Cury said it was "the first time an incident of this type has occurred" on an Eurotunnel loading platform.
The BBC's Evan Davis, who was travelling through the Eurotunnel to Calais at the time of the incident, witnessed blue light vehicles "concentrated on one of the platforms" as he entered France.
"There were plenty of cars queueing up at check-in when I drove past just now, and I saw some cars going through check-in, so despite the collision they weren't being held," he said from the scene.
Photos published by localFrench newspaper La Voix du Nord,externalshowed a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers.
Eurostar has released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel.
"This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected."
The Eurotunnel runs under the sea between England and France, from Folkestone in Kent to Coquelles on the French side.
Three different rail services operate through the tunnel - the Eurostar, a passenger train that begins in London and goes to several European destinations, freight trains which transport goods and Le Shuttle, which transports vehicles.

title: Maduro pleads not guilty to new torture-related charges in New York
summary: "I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in court, responding to newly added torture-related charges.
body:
Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are seen in a federal court in New York in July.
Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture.
The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week.
Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail.
The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027.
In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured.
Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony against me."
"I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator.
Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro.
"I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator.
Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn.
The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states.
The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system.
Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.
He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal.
Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.

title: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
summary: Children were buried under the debris after the roof crashed through three classrooms, police say.
body:
On the ground in Pakistan as school roof collapse kills more than 30 children
At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.
More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition.
Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC.
The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris.
Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes".
Warning: This article contains distressing details
An English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances.
Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said.
"I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away."
"There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water."
Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels".
A rescue worker said an upper-floor roof collapsed, crashing through three classrooms
The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak.
Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down.
There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.
It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.
Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.
The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals.
Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead.
The police chief said the building was still "extremely dangerous" and urged people to move away.
The Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Faisal Karim Kundi, has ordered a safety audit of all schools in the province to "identify potential risks and ensure that immediate corrective measures are taken wherever necessary".
"We cannot allow the safety of our children to be compromised," he said.
Furious family members of deceased pupils accused the school of ignoring safety concerns. "Make an example of them, a lesson for all," Mohammad Zaman, a man who lost two nephews in the disaster, told Reuters news agency.

In June,fourteen children died after the roof of a private tuition centre near Lahorecollapsed.
And in August, 14 newborn babies were killed by a fire that ripped through a neonatal unit at a hospital in the capital, Islamabad, which an inquiry foundlacked fire alarms and sprinklers.

title: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
summary: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect to be "on the menu" in the chancellor's Budget tax later this month.
body:
Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time.
John Healey has described the banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, yet has refused to rule out a raid on the sector.
The biggest four banks collectively made around £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, leading to calls from trade unions and others for additional taxes.
However, the banking sector trade body, UK Finance, warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax, plus a levy on the assets held on their balance sheets.
The sector contributed nearly £40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in.
The bank levy generated £1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further £1.2bn.
There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.
The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around £2bn a year.
The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.
In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.
In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.
There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.
Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.
It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.
However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.
Whatever form it takes, banks believe the chancellor now has much more of an appetite to take a larger slice of their pie.

title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
summary: After Primark announced plans for home delivery, we hear from women who never go into clothes stores.
body:
Jess says returning online purchases is less hassle than shopping in person
Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online.
As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says.
"The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.
Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".
And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".
Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.
But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark nowplans to launch a home delivery service in Britain.
Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.
The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.
Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.
Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic.
Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019.
Internet shopping has also been boosted by thedecline of the High Streetin many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town."
Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online.
"I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says.
"I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important."
Julia does most of her shopping online, but likes going into book stores
Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted.
The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces."
Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically.
"I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed."
The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule.
Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".
However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete.
"Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks.
"When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."
But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have startedcharging a fee if customers make frequent returns.
This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor".
"Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."

title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
summary: The culture secretary says the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
body:
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.
Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal.
"We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.
ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries".
The two companies announced in Julythat Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.
The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.
What Sky buying ITV could mean for your favourite shows
But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up.
In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including:
The need for free expression of opinion in news media
The need for a range of views in news media across the UK
The need for a range of people controlling the media across the UK
The need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UK
The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV.
Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.
But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.
The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.
This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.
Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns.
A Sky spokesperson said: "We havealready made clear commitmentsto protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."
An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process.
"This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."
Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.
This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.
She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."

title: AI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debut
summary: It comes as some investors have become concerned about the amount of money being spent on AI infrastructure.
body:
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic has been drumming up support for its expected stock market listing as it seeks to reassure investors of its profit-making potential.
Anthropic revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.
In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on tech.
It also emphasised safety at its event after warnings by current and former researchers of serious and even existential risks to humanity posed by AI.
Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.
The company also told investors during the event at its headquarters in San Francisco that it had made a third quarter profit on an adjusted basis, an accounting method which ignores non-recurring costs.
Investors reportedly left the Anthropic investor event optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability.
Alongside concerns about profit generation, there have also been fears about the safety of AI models.
Anthropic has been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodeicalling on the pace of development to slow down.
In September one of its researchers warned of a greater than 10% chance that AI could "kill all humans"within the next decade, and a former researcher said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened"about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.
The firm itself said in September it had identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" whichcould support the development of biological weapons.
However, US President Donald Trump has said researchers have been "bringing up things that won't happen" and that in a race between the US and China to develop the technology, "whoever wins AI, wins".
Rival tech firm OpenAI has also warned about safety, with its chief executive Sam Altman saying in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns.
The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.

'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire
Anthropic's revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, are an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.
Stocks in some US technology companies dropped on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.
Shares in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.
In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank were down by more than 9% on Thursday. South Korean semiconductor giants also dropped, with Samsung fallingby 9.5% and SK Hynix 11% lower.
Shares have been falling this week after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.
Tan said at a conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".
The falls deepened after US inflation data released on Wednesday showed price rises accelerated by more than expected in September.
Investors are concerned that higher inflation will mean the US Federal Reserve is more likely to put up the cost of borrowing.

title: 'I paid thousands to a company for jobs that never came'
summary: Apurv Patel is one of several people who say they were promised job opportunities that did not appear.
body:
Apurv Patel said he paid Synetal Solutions £3,600 and claimed he was verbally promised a guaranteed sponsored job
A company has been accused of promising jobs in the healthcare sector which never materialised, leaving people thousands of pounds out of pocket.
Registered in 2025, Synetal Solutions Ltd says it offers career-focused training programmes in the healthcare and IT sectors.
But the BBC has spoken to a number of people who claim they were promised training and support to secure sponsored healthcare jobs that never became available to apply for.
London Citizens Advice says it has seen an increase in recruitment-related scams since the governmentstopped overseas recruitment for care workers,external. The charity described the firm's practices as "unethical".
Synetal Solutions says it "takes these concerns seriously and disputes the broad allegation that its services or candidate outcomes are fictitious".
Apurv Patel, who has been in the UK on a Skilled Worker visa since 2023, said he paid Synetal Solutions £3,600 across February and March for healthcare training after he and a friend were verbally promised guaranteed sponsored jobs.
Eight months later he has received no job offers, interviews or meaningful employment support, he said.
"I'm frustrated. I paid money, I wasted my time. I did whatever they wanted without any result," he said.
"It's had a miserable effect on my family and finances."
Patel said he did receive some training but described it as poor quality and ultimately "worthless".
Having previously worked for two years as a healthcare assistant, he said he became concerned when a trainer was unable to answer routine questions about care work.
"She didn't give us any answers and we realised she didn't have any experience of healthcare," he said.
The company disputes claims that training was ineffective.
He also alleged communication with the company deteriorated after he made his second payment, with responses sometimes taking several days.
Patel has since complained to his bank and sought help from Citizens Advice.
The BBC has seen emails from the company advertising a "three-month recruitment programme" offering "training and placement with sponsorship" for £5,500.
Home Office guidance,externalstates agencies may charge for services such as training or CV-writing assistance, but cannot charge fees solely for finding, or attempting to find, employment.
Responding to questions about its marketing, Synetal Solutions said: "We acknowledge the 'guarantee' wording in the emails supplied and recognise that contractual terms alone do not resolve concerns about those assurances."
As part of its programme, Synetal Solutions created accounts for trainees on iHasco, a health and social care training platform.
The BBC contacted iHasco, which confirmed the company was a customer. However, it said its terms did not permit customers to resell its training content to individuals who were not employees.
The company said it was reviewing Synetal Solutions' account and would take appropriate action if necessary.
Synetal Solutions said it had acted in accordance with its agreement with iHasco.
The Care Quality Commission said there was no single qualification that automatically qualified someone to work as a care worker. Instead, providers are responsible for ensuring employees are appropriately trained and competent for their roles.
The BBC also contacted a number of healthcare organisations whose logos appeared on Synetal Solutions' website as examples of employers where graduates had worked.
Those organisations that responded said they had no links to the company. Some also said they had not authorised the use of their branding, and some said they would not accept certificates provided through the company's training.
Daniel Blake says the way Synetal Solutions has operated is unethical
Daniel Blake, director of London Citizens Advice, described the company's approach as "exploitative".
"The promises that were made are impossible promises," he said. "They are targeting people with vulnerable immigration status.
"This company is asking for large sums of money upfront without any reputable standards, without any reputable evidence of success, and yet when it goes wrong they are refusing to take any responsibility.
"For us, it seems a very unethical way of conducting business."
He added that no reputable recruitment agency would guarantee a successful outcome without first assessing a candidate and matching them to a suitable role, and urged anybody asked to pay large sums upfront to seek independent advice.
"If it seems too good to be true, it probably is," he said.
The company's website stated: "Synetal Solutions provides the right support, guidance, and guaranteed job placement to help you succeed."
But since the BBC contacted Synetal Solutions mentions of job guarantees were removed from the website.
Its social media channels also promoted healthcare as "one of the most reliable paths" for people seeking visa-sponsored work in the UK.
The website previously promised applicants a job - but this has since been removed
Sarah and Rahul, whose names we have changed, said they paid £3,000 to Synetal Solutions while seeking sponsored employment before the expiry of their student visas.
Rahul, a former dentist in India, could remain in the UK on a graduate visa for longer, but Sarah's immigration status was close to expiring.
To pay the fee, the couple said they borrowed money from a family friend and took out a loan.
Rahul said he was shocked by the quality of the training.
"The mentor didn't know anything about healthcare," he said.
The couple said they were also shown the names of established healthcare providers, including Bupa, as examples of potential employers. Bupa told the BBC it had no connection with the company.
Synetal Solutions says some of their candidates "told us they had secured employment with Bupa" and the reference was "not intended to suggest a formal partnership with Bupa".
It says it had not verified those outcomes and "cannot attribute the recruitment decisions to our training".
Rahul said he secured one or two interviews, but prospective employers rejected the certificates he had received through the programme.
The couple said Synetal Solutions had since stopped responding to their messages.
"We're desperate," Sarah said. "We don't see any other way out."
Amisha - not her real name - says her certificates were rejected as invalid by one company she had an interview with
Amisha, whose name has also been changed, said she signed up with Synetal after being told that both a placement and visa sponsorship were guaranteed.
Her student visa is due to expire soon.
She said the training consisted of three sessions lasting around 90 minutes each.
After paying an initial instalment of £1,800, she became reluctant to make a second payment because she felt she had received little in return. She said the company warned her that her contract would be cancelled if she failed to pay, prompting her to transfer a further £1,800.
"I was waiting for interviews for two or three months. They were ignoring me," she said.
According to Amisha, the company applied for only a handful of vacancies advertised on job-search website Indeed. She eventually secured an interview for a healthcare assistant role, but said the employer told her the certificates she had received were not recognised.
A screenshot of a supposed testimonial from Synetal Solutions' website with content that does not appear to make sense
The BBC also identified what appeared to be at least a couple of stock photographs or AI-generated images used as testimonials on the company's website.
The company said it had not authenticated the two reviews identified, and removed them after we contacted them.
Teni Shahiean, an immigration lawyer at OTS Solicitors, said the promises being made to individuals facing visa deadlines were "particularly concerning"
Teni Shahiean, an immigration lawyer at OTS Solicitors, said it was "particularly concerning" where individuals facing visa deadlines were being asked to make substantial payments on the understanding that jobs, sponsorship or immigration outcomes were seemingly guaranteed.
She urged caution, adding that a job offer alone does not guarantee someone will be able to remain in the UK.
"The outcome can depend on the role, the sponsor, the individual meeting the relevant immigration requirements and, ultimately, any decision by the Home Office," she said.
Blake told the BBC: "If it seems good to be true, it probably is. If you are considering handing over money upfront then seek advice."
He said that "if people have given money and haven't received the service that they were entitled to they should seek redress".
"First of all, make a complaint directly to the company, then to Trading Standards.
"If people feel a criminal offence has happened, we would encourage and support them to go to the police."
A government spokesperson said: "We know how much distress scammers cause to their victims, which is why we will do everything in our power to protect hardworking families and vulnerable customers.
"Our reforms have provided Companies House with new and improved powers to prevent companies from acting unlawfully and to query, remove and share suspicious information."
Synetal Solutions said: "We provide training and employment assistance and maintain supporting records. Recruitment, sponsorship and visa decisions depend on employers and the Home Office."
The company said it had records of genuine candidates who had secured jobs and sponsorship through its services.

The bank levy generated £1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further £1.2bn.
There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.
The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around £2bn a year.
The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.
In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.
In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.
There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.
Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.
It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.
However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.
Whatever form it takes, banks believe the chancellor now has much more of an appetite to take a larger slice of their pie.

title: Equality watchdog writes to Greens over 'Zionism is racism' motion
summary: The party was reported to the Equality and Human Rights Commission by MPs and antisemitism campaigners.
body:
Green leader Zack Polanski said the motion was 'imperfect' but supported the substance of it
The equality watchdog has written to the Green Party asking for more information about a controversial "Zionism is racism" motion passed by members.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said it recognised that "many Jewish people will be feeling vulnerable" following the motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month.
The motion described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".
In a response to the ECHR letter, the party said it "will not discriminate against or exclude people for holding Zionist views" and was committed to tackling antisemitism.
Dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners wrote to the regulator raising concerns about antisemitism after the Green motion was passed.
Alongside Jewish groups, the motion was criticised by four of the five Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive".
It piled somepressure on Green leader Zack Polanskiin the wake of a by-election defeat. He said the motion was "imperfect" and he wanted to see it amended.
Labour has said it willend power-sharing agreementswith the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion.
On Thursday, the EHRC confirmed it had written to the Greens following the complaints received.
A spokesperson for the watchdog said: "We have written to the Green Party of England and Wales about its recently adopted 'Zionism is racism' motion to ask for more information and assess its practical implications and potential impact.
"We have received complaints alleging unlawful activity under the Equality Act 2010, including concerns that Jewish people could face discrimination because of their beliefs following the adoption of the motion."
The watchdog said it would "take action where appropriate" after assessing the extra information.
"In the case of the Green Party motion, compliance with the Equality Act is likely to hinge on the practical effects of the motion," the spokesperson added.
In a letter earlier this month, some MPs raised concerns not only about the motion itself but also amendments to protect Jewish Green members at Zionist synagogues being voted down.
"Taken together, these developments raise serious questions about whether Jewish members can participate freely and equally in the party, and whether their religious and communal connections could expose them to complaints or disciplinary action," their letter said.
Separately, the Campaign Against Antisemitism wrote to the EHRC alleging the party had breached the Equality Act through discrimination against Jews.
The campaign group said the motion "effectively states that the state of Israel should not exist" and "defines support for a Jewish homeland in any form as racist".
Having been backed by members, the motion has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.
In response to the EHRC letter, the Green Party of England and Wales said it "will not discriminate against or exclude people for holding Zionist views" and the motion sets out a political position with "no impact on membership conditions or internal disciplinary processes".
"The party's comprehensive antisemitism guidance, which forms part of our framework of ethics, remains unchanged," a spokesperson added.
"We remain committed to tackling antisemitism and ensuring Jewish members feel welcome and respected."

title: Farage defends Reform's vetting after councillors filmed making racist comments
summary: The Reform leader says "you can't vet for future comments", after undercover filming of party activists.
body:
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.
Nigel Farage has insisted Reform UK does not have an issue with vetting, after ITV News broadcast undercover filming of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.
The Reform leader told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments".
In the film,Undercover: A Year in Reform,external, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".
ITV's filming, gathered over a year, involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total.
Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.
Two years ago,Farage vowed to root out "bad apples" among Reform's candidates, saying "bigots" and "extremists" were not welcome.
Defending the party's vetting processes, Farage told BBC Look East: "You can't vet for future comments. You can look at someone's CV. You can look at someone's social media...
"I can't predict what they're going to say after a drink, when they're being provoked by somebody or egged on to say something."
Pressed over whether the party had an issue with vetting, he said: "No, not at all. We actually vet to a much higher standard than the other parties."
He insisted "appropriate action" would be taken following the broadcast, but added: "I'm promising you, however heavily you vet, you cannot stop what people say in the future."
Watch: Reform UK councillor filmed making racist comments, ITV investigation shows
ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.
These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, after defecting from the Conservative Party in 2025.
Feeney, Solihull's deputy mayor, told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites".
Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than 1% of British population can be non-white."
Farage said "the most egregious case" in ITV's filming was "somebody who is a long-term Conservative councillor", in an apparent reference to Feeney.
He said "anyone who says stuff like that" was "not welcome".
The Reform UK leader added: "But I promise you, if an undercover investigation spoke to hundreds of Labour councillors or Conservative councillors or however many hundreds they spoke to, and you provoke people, you'll find unsavoury things said by all parties."

On a different day in the ITV broadcast, Feeney is joined by two other Reform candidates, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, who discuss speculation of a mosque being built in the local area.
"There's got to be a way of stopping them - like, go and buy some pork chops; we'll bury it in the ground," Campbell is heard saying in the film.
Whelan says "we'll take pictures of it", prompting Feeney to add: "I was gonna say, 'Unfortunately, this is a pig cemetery, mate'."
Discussing a female Reform candidate from Birmingham, Feeney is heard saying, "I didn't know where to look", before Whelan adds: "I'd have been sniffing that seat as soon as she got up."
The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons" and would be continuing as an independent councillor.
The BBC has contacted Campbell and Whelan, who has resigned as a councillor, for a response.
A Reform UK Solihull spokesman condemned Feeney and Whelan's "misogynistic and offensive comments" and confirmed they were no longer Reform councillors.
The spokesman said Campbell's comment "was a joke in poor taste but with no malicious intent", adding: "It's something that he deeply regrets, and the party will not be taking any further action."
Elsewhere in the film, Dean Miller, a councillor in the south London borough of Bromley, is shown campaigning for Reform in the Makerfield by-election.
"We've been ethnically cleansed out of London because you never used to get any blacks over in Bromley," he tells an ITV undercover reporter. "And now, you know, Bromley's like massive Nigerian communities there."
Miller says he is "not racist", before later adding: "The Muslim thing, that is going to be that thing that takes over everything and then everyone just has one religion. Because, apparently, King Charles is a [expletive] Muslim... I think that's [expletive] traitorous."
ITV reported that Miller would now sit as an independent councillor having resigned from Reform and had told them in a statement that he was heavily medicated due to a chronic pain condition when he made the comments.
The BBC has contacted him for comment.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Reform should take "immediate and firm action against those who've been revealed to be making these abhorrent comments".
He added: "There is no place for any form of racism, antisemitism, discrimination in British politics, and we all should be relentless in repeating that and taking the firmest possible action."
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "We should be asking why there's so many stories like this of people in Reform who are making these appalling comments."
Asked about one of the individuals being a former Tory councillor, she said: "It's not my problem anymore."
Badenoch added: "I don't want people like that in the Conservative Party. I'm glad they have gone."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."
A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

title: Burnham asks for his Widdecombe remarks to be corrected
summary: The prime minister had faced calls to apologise for his comments about the alleged murder of the former minister.
body:
Andy Burnham has asked for Parliament's official record to be corrected after telling MPs an "individual" was "responsible for the murder" of Ann Widdecombe.
The prime minister had faced calls to apologise for the remarks, made during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, with a senior Tory saying they breached the "presumption of innocence" in criminal cases.
A man was charged with Widdecombe's murder in July, but is yet to enter a plea for the charge and is not due to stand trial until next year.
A No 10 spokeswoman said a correction had been issued to Hansard, the official report of parliamentary debates, and would be "published in due course".
Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform spokeswoman.
A trial before a High Court judge is scheduled for 8 June next year, and a plea and case management hearing on 29 January.
Earlier this month, Kerry was also charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
Speaking on Thursday, Conservative shadow Commons leader Jesse Norman accused Burnham of breaching Parliament's sub judice rule, which says MPs should not refer to pending court cases in order to avoid influencing the outcome.
He added that the prime minister's comments at PMQs had "breached the legal presumption of innocence".
He asked Commons leader Sir Alan Campbell, a government minister, to "correct the record, withdraw the remark and apologise on behalf of the prime minister".
In response, Sir Alan said the prime minister had "said that he misspoke, he has apologised and he has corrected the record".
"There is no excuse for misspeaking in the House and I am not trying to explain that away, but this prime minister is characterised by an authenticity and a passion in the way that he responds," he added.
"It is not unusual for prime ministers or anybody else to misspeak in the House.
"As long as they correct the record, which he has done, that should be put into perspective."

title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
summary: The home secretary said she would not hesitate to impose measures on other countries "refusing to co-operate".
body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.
From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.
Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.
Eritrea branded the move a "perfunctory political gimmick", saying the UK had not issued a single visa to an Eritrean official since 2023,which the Home Office denies.
The country's embassy in London also accused the UK of refusing to engage in "meaningful and appropriate dialogue".
It said the UK had failed to disclose the return of criminals still serving prison terms and that the UK had claimed returns were voluntary "when clearly, they were not".
However, a Home office spokesperson said the Eritrean government's commentary  "misrepresents the UK's position".
The UK had granted an exemption from immigration control for an Eritrean official in August 2026, according to the Home Office. Sources also said the UK hoped to restore co-operation between the two countries.
Human Rights Watch has accused Eritrea's government of widespread repression - including forced labour, conscription and restrictions on freedom of expression.
Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June -accounting for 18% of arrivals,external, according to figures from the House of Commons Library.
Mahmood said: "Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused."
She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".
The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.
The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission.
The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.
In the 12 months to June only seven people from Eritrea were returned there from the UK, according to Home Office figures. A further 244 Eritreans were returned to other countries.
Over the same period, more than 5,800 Eritreans arrived in the UK via small boats. A further 1,300 were given visas, mostly to join people already settled in the UK.
Dr Madeleine Sumption, director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said targeting Eritrea would have little impact.
"Eritrea is one of the major countries of origin for asylum seekers coming to the UK - we had roughly 7,000 asylum applications in the last year of data, roughly 8% of the total," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"Most Eritreans who come and claim asylum are not removable at all - the government would never be in negotiations to remove them because 84% are successful at initial decision; more will be successful on appeal."
She added that about 1,400 people were initially refused asylum, but that this number would reduce after appeals.
Many young Eritreans try to leave the country - which is a one-party state - to avoid military conscription, which can last for decades.
Eritrea has never held an election since independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and there is no independent media. Critics of President Isaias Afwerki have been arrested and jailed for many years, often without trial.
Only four religions are permitted in the country – Orthodox Christianity, Sunni Islam, the Roman Catholic Church, and the Evangelical-Lutheran church of Eritrea – and followers of other religions have been locked up for years on end.
Last November, the Home Office said it was prepared to suspend visas from countries that "fail to co-operate with the return of their citizens".
Earlier this year, the UK threatened visa restrictions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of  Congo (DRC).
Restrictions wereannounced against the DRClast year, but the Home Office said these have beenlifted after co-operation on returnsimproved.
Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced.
But Sumption pointed out that the government may avoid targeting certain countries to avoid damaging trade relationships.
"If you're looking at overall numbers of people who are refused asylum and not returned to their country of origin, it would be places like Pakistan, also Bangladesh that are right at the top of the list," she said.
"But the collateral damage of a ban on visas for those countries when you have so many international students coming, for example, [and] a lot of people coming on work visas would be much greater than a country like Eritrea."
According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year.
There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year.
Of those who had been returned, fewer than 6,000 have been convicted of a criminal offence.
The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave.
This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily.
People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation.
There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year.
That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.
Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026:
5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat
People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026.
Up until September the UK wastrialing a scheme with Franceto return people who arrived in the country on a small boat.
For every person the UK sent back to France, the UK accepted a number of asylum seekers.
This was called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people were returned through this arrangement.
Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers.
All other returns are "voluntary". This means a person has agreed to leave and may receive government help with travel and other costs to help facilitate the return.
Some people classed as leaving the country voluntarily do so completely independently and withoutany government knowledge or involvement.
Independent returns made up 34% of the total from July 2025 to June 2026.
